# unbuned

Extract JavaScript from Bun-compiled executables.

Source: https://github.com/vibheksoni/unbuned
Site: https://vibheksoni.github.io/unbuned/
License: MIT

## Read the JavaScript inside any Bun executable.

A Bun app is just JavaScript wrapped up in a binary. unbuned takes the wrapper off and writes the
JavaScript to a file you can open, search and read.

One Python file. Nothing to install. Python 3.6 or newer. Windows, macOS and Linux.

## One file in. JavaScript out.

unbuned is a single Python file. You point it at an executable, and it gives you back the JavaScript that
app was built from. It does not decompile anything, because it does not have to: the code is already in
there, just hidden behind a section header and a lot of binary noise.

Find the bundle: looks inside the .exe, .app or Linux binary for the section where Bun keeps the app.

Cut away the binary: walks through the files in that section and works out where the code stops and the
data starts.

Write the JavaScript: saves the result exactly as it found it, so nothing is quietly changed on the way
out.

Ask for everything with --all, and you get the whole tree:

    output/claude/claude.js              all the JavaScript
    output/claude/manifest.json          what is in each file
    output/claude/modules/               one file per part
    output/claude/sources/               the original source
    output/claude/assets/                images and other files
    output/claude/claude.bytecode-*.bin  the code Bun compiled

## Built for the moment a Bun app lands on your disk and you just want to read it.

Most of the time you want the JavaScript, fast, without setting up a whole reversing project first. So:
clone it, run one command, and get a file you can search straight away.

Nothing to install: one file, standard library only, Python 3.6 or newer. No pip install and no build
step to get through before you can look at a file.

Real file names: Bun keeps a list of every file it packed in. unbuned reads that list, so you get names
like 0006-cli.js instead of chunk-9fxe9jf7.js.

Output you can trust: the file is written byte for byte, exactly as it was inside the binary. Formatting
only changes the layout, never the code.

Please use it for reverse engineering, security research, malware analysis, learning and recovery work.
Respect the licence of what you are looking at, and the law where you are.

## Example run

    $ python unbuned.py droid.exe

    Extracted: output/droid/droid.js
    Size: 14,102,812 bytes
    Container: pe (.bun section, 41,171,402 bytes at offset 114079744)
    JavaScript: 14,102,812 bytes at section offset 31
    Modules: 1
    Module graph: 20 embedded files
    Entry point: B:/~BUN/root/droid.exe
    Sources: 4331 original files recovered from 1 source maps

## Five real apps, opened up.

These are real extractions, committed to the repository so you can see the result before you run
anything. Click any of them to open the file on GitHub.

- Claude Code, Anthropic. claude.exe, 40.9 MB, 2,156 files. The agent, the CLI and every tool it ships
  with, all named the way Bun recorded them.
  https://github.com/vibheksoni/unbuned/blob/master/output/claude/claude.js
- Factory Droid, Factory. droid.exe, 14.1 MB, 1 file. Agent logic, model settings and the app flows. A
  newer build of Droid unpacks into 623 files.
  https://github.com/vibheksoni/unbuned/blob/master/output/droid/droid.js
- Freebuff, Freebuff. freebuff, 11.4 MB, 1 file. The telemetry, model routing and product flows that ship
  inside the desktop app.
  https://github.com/vibheksoni/unbuned/blob/master/output/freebuff/freebuff.js
- Slate, Random Labs. slate.exe, 22.4 MB, 2 files. No public source anywhere, so reading it meant taking
  it apart. An OpenCode fork.
  https://github.com/vibheksoni/unbuned/blob/master/output/slate/slate.js
- Claude Agent SDK, Anthropic. claude.exe, 33.8 MB, 3 files. This one runs on compiled bytecode, so what
  comes back is the fallback source, not what runs.
  https://github.com/vibheksoni/unbuned/blob/master/output/claude-sdk/claude.js

## What happens when you run it.

The tricky part is the end. Bun mixes readable text into the data it stores after the code, so a simple
search for the first unreadable byte cuts too early. unbuned starts from the last file it is sure about
and works forwards, so it can only ever leave a little too much, never eat real code.

Work out what kind of file it is: Windows, Mac or Linux. The Mac build can hold several versions in one
file, so unbuned picks the right one.

Find the part Bun uses: every Bun app keeps its code in a section called .bun. unbuned reads the section
table to find it.

Start at the first file: the code begins with a // @bun marker. Starting from a known spot means unbuned
can only ever cut too little, never too much.

Walk through each file: Bun separates the compiled files with a marker and a null byte. unbuned counts
them all and notes where each one starts.

Find where the code stops: it counts the bytes that are not text, then checks for the comments Bun writes
at the end of the code.

Read the list of packed files: Bun stores a list of every file it put in the app, with names, sources and
assets. That is where the real names come from.

Write the file out: the JavaScript is saved exactly as it was, with no re-encoding, and the file is never
loaded fully into memory.

## Getting started.

    git clone https://github.com/vibheksoni/unbuned.git
    cd unbuned

    # take a look first, write nothing
    python unbuned.py claude.exe --inspect

    # now pull the JavaScript out
    python unbuned.py claude.exe

    # or everything at once, formatted to read
    python unbuned.py claude.exe --all --format

It writes to output/claude/claude.js. Open it, search it, or diff it against the next build.

## Every flag

- -o, --output DIR: save somewhere else
- -m, --modules: one file per part, plus a manifest
- --assets: also pull out images and other files
- --sources: also pull out the original source
- --bytecode: also save the compiled code Bun made
- -a, --all: all of the above in one go
- --format: tidy up the code so it is easier to read
- --indent N: spaces per level, default 2
- --wrap-at N: line length, default 100, 0 turns it off
- --inspect: report what is inside without writing anything
- --json: same report, as JSON
- --arch CPU: pick a version from a Mac universal build
- --chunk-size N: how finely to scan, default 1000
- --threshold F: how much non-text ends the code, default 0.3
- --skip-existing: never overwrite a file that is already there
- -q, --quiet: say less

## What people use it for.

Looking inside an app: see how a shipped app works without building a whole decompiler first.

Security research: check a released app for hidden phone-home calls, keys or odd behaviour.

Malware analysis: take apart a suspicious dropper or loader and see what it actually runs.

Recovering lost code: the project is gone but the executable is still around. Get the logic back.

Learning: see how real apps pack up their code and dependencies.

Challenges and CTFs: get to the code fast when the clock is running.

## What it does not do.

Worth saying out loud, because a tool that hides its limits is worse than no tool. None of these are bugs
waiting to be fixed. They are what Bun puts in the file.

JavaScript only: it pulls out the JavaScript and the files packed next to it. It does not touch compiled
machine code.

Names stay as Bun wrote them: a file Bun called chunk-9fxe9jf7.js is still called that. The names are the
real ones, but hashed ones stay hashed.

Original files need source maps: the before-bundling code is only there if the app shipped source maps
with it.

The last file can be cut short: the end of the code is worked out by measuring, so the final line can be
trimmed. Bytecode never sneaks in.

Formatting only moves things around: it never renames, reorders or rewrites code. Very long lines stay
long.

Bytecode stays as bytecode: compiled JavaScriptCore is saved as-is. Turning it back into source is not
something this does.

## Common questions.

What does unbuned actually do? It takes the JavaScript out of an app that was built with Bun. It finds the
.bun part of the file, works out where the code stops and the rest of the data begins, and saves the code
as a normal .js file you can open in any editor.

Do I need to install anything? No. unbuned is one Python file that uses the standard library. If you have
Python 3.6 or newer, you are ready to go. There is nothing to install.

What kinds of files does it work on? Windows .exe files, Mac apps, and Linux binaries built with Bun. If a
file does not have the usual section table, unbuned searches the whole file for Bun markers instead.

Can it get the original source files back? When the app shipped source maps, yes. unbuned unpacks them and
writes the original files into a folder that keeps their real names. Claude Code and Factory Droid both
ship source maps, so thousands of files come back.

How does it know the real file names? Bun writes a list of every file it packed into the app before the
code itself. unbuned reads that list, so files come back with the names they had on the developer machine
instead of made-up ones.

Am I allowed to use it? It is meant for reverse engineering, security research, malware analysis, learning
and recovering your own code. Please respect the licence of the software you look at, any contract you
agreed to, and the law where you live.
